## What Is an Employer of Record in Guyana


An[Employer of Record (EOR)](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-definition-employer-of-record) is a third-party organization that becomes the legal employer of your worker in Guyana, while you keep control of their day-to-day work and performance. The EOR signs the employment contract, runs payroll, and handles statutory filings on your behalf. You manage what the person does. The EOR manages the paperwork that makes hiring them in Guyana legal.


This distinction matters because a foreign company without a registered local entity generally cannot run payroll in Guyana, withhold and remit National Insurance Scheme (NIS) contributions, or issue an employment contract that holds up under local labor law. You either set up a Guyanese entity yourself, or use one of the[best EOR companies](https://www.bolto.com/blog/best-eor-companies-global-hiring-guide) that already has the legal standing to hire workers there.


For a company hiring one person, or a handful of people, in Guyana, an EOR is typically the faster, lower-risk route. Setting up a local entity takes time, money, and ongoing legal upkeep, a heavy commitment for a single hire. An EOR skips that step: your employee gets a compliant contract, gets paid correctly, and gets their NIS contributions handled, without you opening a Guyanese subsidiary.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Guyana


Before you extend an offer in Guyana, it helps to know the rules that come with it. Local labor law sets real requirements around contracts, statutory contributions, and termination, and getting them wrong can mean fines, back pay, or a contract that does not hold up if challenged.


Guyana’s employment relationships are governed primarily by the Labour Act, which sets baseline standards for working hours, termination notice, and related protections, alongside sector-specific ordinances that can add requirements depending on the industry. Under Guyana’s National Insurance Scheme framework, employers are generally required to register with the[National Insurance Scheme](https://www.nis.org.gy/information_on_contributions) (NIS) and remit both employer and employee contributions each pay period, since NIS funds sickness, maternity, and pension benefits for the workforce. Employment contracts in Guyana typically spell out wages, working hours, and termination terms in a way that holds up under Guyanese labor law, and probationary periods are common practice before a role converts to permanent status. Termination generally calls for[advance notice or pay in lieu](https://labour.gov.gy/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Termination-and-severance.pdf) , with the exact period tied to how long the employee has been with the company, and severance can apply in redundancy situations. Because these requirements can shift and enforcement varies by sector, most foreign companies lean on local counsel or an EOR to keep contracts and NIS filings current instead of tracking every change themselves.


**Key compliance requirements to track in Guyana:**


- Labour Act and sector-specific ordinances setting baseline rules on working hours, termination notice, and related protections
- NIS registration, with employer and employee contributions remitted each pay period
- Employment contracts that spell out wages, working hours, and termination terms, typically paired with a probationary period
- Termination notice or pay in lieu tied to tenure, with severance owed in redundancy situations
